rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says his mother carried him for two years and he was born with his teeth already grown.
rows.anchor: الضحاك: وضعتني أمي وقد حملت بي في بطنها سنتين

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: A report attributed to Malik says he was carried for two years; another view gives three years.
rows.anchor: مالك أنه حمل به في بطن أمه سنتين، وقيل: ثلاث سنين

rows.speaker: محمد بن عجلان
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Ajlan was reportedly carried for three years; after his mother died, his moving fetus was removed by opening her abdomen, and he had teeth.
rows.anchor: إن محمد بن عجلان مكث في بطن أمه ثلاث سنين، فماتت به

rows.speaker: حماد بن سلمة
rows.claim: Hammad ibn Salama says Hurm ibn Hayyan was named Hurm because he remained in his mother's womb for four years.
rows.anchor: حماد بن سلمة: إنما سمي هرم بن حيان هرما لأنه بقي في بطن أمه أربع سنين

rows.speaker: الغزنوي
rows.claim: Al-Ghaznawi says al-Dahhak was born after two years with teeth showing, which is why he was named al-Dahhak.
rows.anchor: الغزنوي أن الضحاك ولد لسنتين، وقد طلعت سنه

rows.speaker: عباد بن العوام
rows.claim: Abbad ibn al-Awwam recounts a neighbor giving birth after four years to a boy with shoulder-length hair; a passing bird said, “Kash.”
rows.anchor: عباد بن العوام: ولدت جارة لنا لأربع سنين غلاما شعره إلى منكبيه

rows.speaker: ابن خويز منداد
rows.claim: Ibn Khuzaym Mindad says the minimum and maximum of pregnancy, menstruation, and postpartum bleeding are established by legal reasoning because God reserved their exact knowledge; observed rare cases can set limits.
rows.anchor: ابن خويز منداد: أقل الحيض والنفاس وأكثره وأقل الحمل وأكثره مأخوذ من طريق الاجتهاد

rows.speaker: الطبائعيون
rows.claim: The naturalists whom Ibn al-Arabi criticizes claim seven planets govern gestation in turn, with the Sun causing movement in month four and Saturn chilling the fetus in month eight.
rows.anchor: وهم الطبائعيون الذين يزعمون أن مدبر الحمل في الرحم الكواكب السبعة تأخذه شهرا شهرا

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi rejects the claim that maximum gestation is nine months as an unsupported assertion, and mocks the astrologers’ arbitrary return to Saturn after their planetary cycle.
rows.anchor: ابن العربي: نقل بعض المتساهلين من المالكيين أن أكثر الحمل تسعة أشهر وهذا ما لم ينطق به قط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “By a measure” can mean according to increase and decrease.
rows.anchor: وكل شيء عنده بمقدار } يعني من

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation makes the measure the time when a child leaves the womb and the length of its gestation.
rows.anchor: قدر خروج الولد من بطن أمه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatadah applies the measure to provision and lifespan; the commentator says the verse’s general wording includes all these interpretations.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: في الرزق والأجل. والمقدار القدر وعموم الآية يتناول كل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ghayb and al-shahadah are verbal nouns meaning what is absent and what is witnessed; God knows both what creation cannot see and what it sees.
rows.anchor: والشهادة مصدر بمعنى الشاهد فنبه سبحانه على انفراده بعلم الغيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse praises God’s exclusive knowledge of the unseen and hidden; no one may share in that knowledge with Him.
rows.anchor: لا يجوز أن يشاركه في ذلك أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Physicians may infer from indications and signs, but claiming certainty from them is unbelief; treating them as experience is acceptable because custom can fail while knowledge cannot change.
rows.anchor: وإن قالوا إنها تجربة تركوا وما هم عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kabir means that everything is beneath Him.
rows.anchor: و { الكبير } الذي كل شيء دونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Mutaʿali is exalted above the polytheists’ claims and prevails over everything through power and domination.
rows.anchor: عما يقول المشركون، المستعلي على كل شيء بقدرته وقهره

words: مَّنْ أَسَرَّ ٱلْقَوْلَ وَمَنْ جَهَرَ بِهِۦ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Secret speech is what a person tells himself, while open speech is what he tells someone else; God knows hidden and public good and evil alike.
rows.anchor: إسرار القول: ما حدث به المرء نفسه، والجهر ما حدث به غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One parsing makes min-kum qualify sawāʾ: the one who speaks secretly and the one who speaks openly are equal among you.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون وصفا ل«سواء» التقدير: سر من أسر وجهر من جهر سواء منكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second parsing attaches min-kum to sawāʾ with the sense “equal among you,” as in the construction “I passed by Zayd.”
rows.anchor: على معنى: يستوي منكم، كقولك: مررت بزيد

words: مِّنكُمْ مَّنْ أَسَرَّ ٱلْقَوْلَ وَمَنْ جَهَرَ بِهِۦ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third parsing supplies min-kum separately after both clauses: the one who speaks secretly among you and the one who speaks openly among you.
rows.anchor: على تقدير: سر من أسر منكم وجهر من جهر منكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth parsing supplies a deleted noun, meaning that the secret and public speakers are both people of equal standing, like saying Zayd and Amr are just.
rows.anchor: التقدير: ذو سواء منكم من أسر القول ومن جهر به

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes sawāʾ itself as “equal,” requiring no deleted noun.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «سواء» أي مستو، فلا يحتاج إلى تقدير حذف مضاف

words: وَمَنْ هُوَ مُسْتَخْفٍۭ بِٱلَّيْلِ وَسَارِبٌۢ بِٱلنَّهَارِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s knowledge treats secret and public speech equally, as well as the person hidden in darkness and the one visible on the roads.
rows.anchor: أي يستوي في علم الله السر والجهر

rows.speaker: الأخفش وقطرب
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash and Qutrub say the night “hidden” person is actually visible: the verb can mean to make something appear or bring it out, as in their cited line by Imruʾ al-Qays.
rows.anchor: الأخفش وقطرب: المستخفي بالليل الظاهر ومنه خفيت الشيء وأخفيته

rows.speaker: امرؤ القيس
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays’s verse is cited as evidence for the sense “made visible” in akhfaytu.
rows.anchor: امرؤ القيس: خفاهن من أنفاقهن كأنما خفاهن ودق من عشي مجلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sārib can mean concealed, entering a burrow; the expression is used of a wild animal entering its lair.
rows.anchor: والسارب المتواري، أي الداخل سربا ومنه قولهم: انسرب الوحشي إذا دخل في كناسه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses mustakhfin as concealed and sārib as visible.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس: «مستخف» مستتر، «وسارب» ظاهر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets the hidden person as one concealed in sins and the sārib as one acting openly.
rows.anchor: مجاهد: «مستخف» بالمعاصي، «وسارب» ظاهر

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi says sārib means one who goes away; saraba, yasrubu, and sarūban mean to depart.
rows.anchor: الكسائي: سرب يسرب سربا وسروبا إذا ذهب

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An anonymous poet’s line about releasing a stallion’s tether witnesses sārib in the sense “going away.”
rows.anchor: الشاعر: وكل أناس قاربوا قيد فحلهم ونحن خلعنا قيده فهو مسارب

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء
rows.claim: Abu Raja says sārib is someone going freely over the earth.
rows.anchor: أبو رجاء: السارب الذاهب على وجهه في الأرض

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A poetic line is cited for saraba as going or traveling, though its poet is unnamed.
rows.anchor: الشاعر: أنى سربت وكنت غير سروب

rows.speaker: القتبي
rows.claim: Al-Qutaybi understands the daytime sārib as quickly going about one’s errands, comparing it to water flowing away.
rows.anchor: القتبي: «سارب بالنهار» أي منصرف في حوائجه بسرعة من قولهم انسرب الماء

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Asmaʿi explains the expression “leave his sarb” as leave him his way or path.
rows.anchor: الأصمعي: خل سربه أي طريقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentator says the meaning of Alif Lam Ra has already been explained.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { الر كتاب أنزلناه إليك } تقدم معناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet brings people out by means of the revealed Book, the Qurʾan, through calling them to it.
rows.anchor: أي بالكتاب، وهو القرآن، أي بدعائك إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The darknesses are disbelief, error, and ignorance; the light is faith and knowledge, with disbelief figuratively likened to darkness and Islam to light.
rows.anchor: أي من ظلمات الكفر والضلالة والجهل إلى نور الإيمان والعلم وهذا على التمثيل

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation gives the parallel transitions as innovation to Sunnah and doubt to certainty; the commentator says the meaning is close.
rows.anchor: وقيل: من البدعة إلى السنة، ومن الشك إلى اليقين والمعنى متقارب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By their Lord’s permission means by His granting success and showing them kindness.
rows.anchor: أي بتوفيقه إياهم ولطفه بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition bi in “by their Lord’s permission” attaches to the verb “you bring out.”
rows.anchor: والباء في «بإذن ربهم» متعلقة ب«تخرج»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The action is attributed to the Prophet because he calls, warns, and guides people.
rows.anchor: وأضيف الفعل إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لأنه الداعي والمنذر الهادي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aziz and al-Hamid modify one and the same noun without a conjunction, like “I went to Zayd the wise, the noble.”
rows.anchor: هو كقولك: خرجت إلى زيد العاقل الفاضل من غير واو، لأنهما شيء واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aziz is glossed as having no equal or likeness; another gloss is that no victor can overcome Him, or that He is inviolable in dominion and sovereignty.
rows.anchor: والله هو العزيز الذي لا مثل له ولا شبيه. وقيل: «العزيز» الذي لا يغلبه غالب. وقيل: «العزيز» المنيع في ملكه وسلطانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Hamid is praised by every tongue and glorified everywhere in every condition.
rows.anchor: «الحميد» أي المحمود بكل لسان، والممجد في كل مكان على كل حال

rows.speaker: مقسم عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Miqsam reports Ibn Abbas’s occasion of revelation: some people believed in Jesus and others rejected him; after Muhammad was sent, Jesus’s former rejecters believed Muhammad, while Jesus’s believers rejected him.
rows.anchor: وروى مقسم عن ابن عباس قال: كان قوم آمنوا بعيسى ابن مريم، وقوم كفروا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “town” Abraham asks God to make secure is Mecca; its explanation was given earlier in al-Baqarah.
rows.anchor: يعني مكة وقد مضى في «البقرة»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ijnubni means put me apart from worshipping idols.
rows.anchor: أي اجعلني جانبا عن عبادتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham means his biological sons; he had eight, and none of them worshipped an idol.
rows.anchor: وأراد بقوله: «بني» بنيه من صلبه وكانوا ثمانية، فما عبد أحد منهم صنما

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes the prayer to be for whichever descendants God intends to guide.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو دعاء لمن أراد الله أن يدعو له

rows.speaker: الجحدري وعيسى
rows.claim: Al-Jahdari and ʿIsa read wa-ajنبnī with a hamza cut, while the meaning remains the same.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجحدري وعيسى «وأجنبني» بقطع الألف والمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forms janabtu, ajnabtu, and jannabtu all convey avoiding or leaving something, including the imperative ajtanibhu.
rows.anchor: يقال: جنبت ذلك الأمر وأجنبته وجنبته إياه فتجانبه واجتنبه أي تركه

rows.speaker: إبراهيم التيمي
rows.claim: In a sermon, Ibrahim al-Taymi warns that no one can feel safe from trial after Abraham prayed to be kept from idols, as his father and people had worshipped them.
rows.anchor: وكان إبراهيم التيمي يقول في قصصه: من يأمن البلاء بعد الخليل حين يقول { واجنبنى وبنى أن نعبد الأصنام }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idols are said figuratively to mislead many because they are the cause of misguidance, though inanimate objects cannot act.
rows.anchor: لما كانت سببا للإضلال أضاف الفعل إليهن مجازا فإن الأصنام جمادات لا تفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following Abraham means following the oneness of God; such a follower belongs to his religion.
rows.anchor: في التوحيد. { فإنه مني } أي من أهل ديني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disobeying Abraham here means persisting in associating partners with God.
rows.anchor: { ومن عصاني } أي أصر على الشرك

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view says Abraham made this prayer before learning that God does not forgive associating partners with Him.
rows.anchor: قيل: قال هذا قبل أن يعرفه الله أن الله لا يغفر أن يشرك به

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view limits the forgiveness to those who repent of disobedience before death.
rows.anchor: وقيل: غفور رحيم لمن تاب من معصيته قبل الموت

rows.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
rows.claim: Muqatil ibn Hayyan says the disobedience meant here is anything short of associating partners with God.
rows.anchor: مقاتل بن حيان: «ومن عصاني» فيما دون الشرك

words: رَّبَّنَآ إِنِّىٓ أَسْكَنتُ مِن ذُرِّيَّتِى بِوَادٍ غَيْرِ ذِى زَرْعٍ
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The Bukhari report from Ibn Abbas recounts Abraham leaving nursing Hajar and Ismail at the House near Zamzam with dates and water, at an empty, waterless valley; Hajar trusted God after confirming the command.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس: أول ما اتخذ النساء المنطق من قبل أم إسمعيل

words: فَٱجْعَلْ أَفْـِٔدَةًۭ مِّنَ ٱلنَّاسِ تَهْوِىٓ إِلَيْهِمْ
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In the same report, Hajar runs seven times between Safa and Marwa as the child suffers from thirst; the Prophet identifies this as the people’s saʿy.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The report says an angel excavated Zamzam at Gabriel’s place, and Hajar gathered water while it flowed; the Prophet says that had she left it, Zamzam would have been a running spring.
rows.anchor: فإذا هي بالملك عند موضع زمزم فبحث بعقبه أو قال بجناحه حتى ظهر الماء

rows.speaker: الملك
rows.claim: The angel reassures Hajar that there is no danger of loss: the boy and his father will build God’s House, and God will not abandon its people.
rows.anchor: فقال لها الملك: لا تخافي الضيعة فإن هاهنا بيت الله يبنيه هذا الغلام وأبوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One may not abandon children and family in a desolate place by appealing to this story, trusting God, or following extreme Sufi claims about true reliance: Abraham acted on God’s command.
rows.anchor: لا يجوز لأحد أن يتعلق بهذا في طرح ولده وعياله بأرض مضيعة اتكالا على العزيز الرحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Sarah’s jealousy after Hajar bore Ismail led Abraham to bring Hajar and the child to Mecca; another says they traveled by Buraq from Syria in one day, all by revelation.
rows.anchor: وقد روي أن سارة لما غارت من هاجر بعد أن ولدت إسمعيل خرج بها إبراهيم عليه السلام إلى مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As God established the place for the honored House and sacred city, He sent the angel to uncover water and make it nourishment.
rows.anchor: لما أراد الله تأسيس الحال، وتمهيد المقام، وخط الموضع للبيت المكرم، والبلد المحرم، أرسل الملك

rows.speaker: أبو ذر
rows.claim: In an authentic report, Abu Dharr says Zamzam water alone sustained him for thirty days and nights; he gained weight and felt no pang of hunger.
rows.anchor: وفي الصحيح: أن أبا ذر رضي الله عنه اجتزأ به ثلاثين بين يوم وليلة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas transmitted by al-Daraqutni says Zamzam serves the drinker’s intention: healing, satiety, or relief from thirst; it is Gabriel’s digging and God’s water for Ismail.
rows.anchor: ماء زمزم لما شرب له

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima reports that Ibn Abbas prayed for beneficial knowledge, abundant provision, and healing from every disease when drinking Zamzam.
rows.anchor: وروي أيضا عن عكرمة قال: كان ابن عباس إذا شرب من زمزم

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi says Zamzam’s promised benefits remain until the Last Day for the sincere person of sound inner character who drinks in trust rather than testing it; God exposes those who experiment.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي: وهذا موجود فيه إلى يوم القيامة لمن صحت نيته، وسلمت طويته

rows.speaker: محمد بن علي الترمذي
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi recounts that on a crowded, dark pilgrimage night he drank deeply from Zamzam to avoid leaving the circumambulation for a need, and the discomfort disappeared until morning.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله محمد بن علي الترمذي وحدثني أبي رحمه الله قال: دخلت الطواف في ليلة ظلماء

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
rows.claim: A report from Abdullah ibn Amr says a spring in Paradise lies at Zamzam from the direction of the corner.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عبد الله بن عمرو: إن في زمزم عينا في الجنة من قبل الركن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min in “some of my descendants” is partitive: Abraham settled some of his descendants, namely Ismail and his mother, since Isaac was in Syria.
rows.anchor: «من» في قوله تعالى: «من ذريتي» للتبعيض أي أسكنت بعض ذريتي يعني إسمعيل وأمه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another grammatical view treats min as an extra particle, yielding “I settled my descendants.”
rows.anchor: وقيل: هي صلة أي أسكنت ذريتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse indicates that the House existed from ancient times, as in reports placing it before the Flood; Abraham attributes it to God because no one else owns it.
rows.anchor: يدل على أن البيت كان قديما على ما روي قبل الطوفان، وقد مضى هذا المعنى في سورة «البقرة»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muharram can mean that acts permitted elsewhere, such as sex, are forbidden there; another view says it is protected from tyrants and violation of its sanctity, as Qatadah and others say.
rows.anchor: ووصفه بأنه محرم، أي يحرم فيه ما يستباح في غيره من جماع واستحلال. وقيل: محرم على الجبابرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer is singled out from the religion because of its merit and rank; it is God’s covenant with His servants.
rows.anchor: خصها من جملة الدين لفضلها فيه، ومكانها منه، وهي عهد الله عند العباد

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet is quoted saying that God prescribed five prayers for His servants.
rows.anchor: خمس صلوات كتبهن الله على العباد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent parsing makes li in li-yuqimu al-salah a purpose particle attached to “I settled.”
rows.anchor: واللام في «ليقيموا الصلاة» لام كي هذا هو الظاهر فيها وتكون متعلقة ب «أسكنت»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, li may be a command particle, as though Abraham asks God to entrust them and enable them to establish prayer.
rows.anchor: ويصح أن تكون لام أمر، كأنه رغب إلى الله أن يأتمنهم و أن يوفقهم لإقامة الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse indicates that prayer in Mecca is superior, since Abraham settled them by the sacred House so they would pray there.
rows.anchor: تضمنت هذه الآية أن الصلاة بمكة أفضل من الصلاة بغيرها لأن معنى «ربنا ليقيموا الصلاة»

rows.speaker: أهل الأثر
rows.claim: Most hadith scholars prefer prayer in the Sacred Mosque to prayer in the Prophet’s Mosque by one hundred prayers, citing Ibn al-Zubayr’s Prophetic report; the commentator calls its wording sound and its transmission trustworthy.
rows.anchor: فذهب عامة أهل الأثر إلى أن الصلاة في المسجد الحرام أفضل من الصلاة في مسجد الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم بمائة صلاة

rows.speaker: أبو عمر
rows.claim: Abu Umar authenticates the Ibn al-Zubayr report through Habib al-Muallim from Ata: Yahya ibn Maʿin, Ahmad, and Abu Zurʿa call Habib trustworthy, and Abu Hatim al-Busti includes the report in his Sahih; the commentator treats it as decisive evidence.
rows.anchor: وقد خرج حديث حبيب المعلم هذا عن عطاء بن أبي رباح عن عبد الله بن الزبير عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Abu Umar also cites a similar Prophetic report from Ibn Umar via Musa al-Juhani and Nafi; Musa is deemed trustworthy and praised by al-Qattan, Ahmad, and Yahya.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عمر: وقد روي عن ابن عمر عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم مثل حديث ابن الزبير

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The prophetic report traced to Jabir in the preceding segment says prayer in the Prophet’s Mosque is better than a thousand elsewhere, while prayer in the Sacred Mosque is better than one hundred thousand elsewhere.
rows.anchor: صلاة في مسجدي هذا أفضل من ألف صلاة فيما سواه إلا المسجد الحرام وصلاة في المسجد الحرام أفضل من مائة ألف فيما سواه

rows.speaker: حكيم بن سيف
rows.claim: Hakim ibn Sayf’s Jabir transmission is judged by Abu Umar to be acceptable; if its narrator preserved it, these are two reports, otherwise Habib al-Muallim’s wording prevails.
rows.anchor: وحكيم بن سيف هذا شيخ من أهل الرقة قد روى عنه أبو زرعة الرازي، وأخذ عنه ابن وضاح

rows.speaker: أبو عمر
rows.claim: Abu Umar says the cited reports decisively settle the dispute for anyone guided rightly and free of partisanship.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عمر: وهذا كله نص في موضع الخلاف قاطع له عند من ألهم رشده، ولم تمل به عصبيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Afʾidah is the plural of fuʾad, meaning hearts; the word fuʾad can stand for qalb, as the quoted poem demonstrates.
rows.anchor: الأفئدة جمع فؤاد وهي القلوب، وقد يعبر عن القلب بالفؤاد كما قال الشاعر

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The cited poet’s line uses fuʾad for the heart and shows it being led by longing.
rows.anchor: وإن فؤادا قادني بصبابة إليك على طول المدى لصبور

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view derives afʾidah from wafd, “delegation”: from the original awfidah, the fa is advanced and the waw changes to ya, yielding “delegations of people.”
rows.anchor: وقيل: جمع وفد، والأصل أوفدة، فقدمت الفاء وقلبت الواو ياء كما هي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hawiya means to incline toward; the verb also describes a she-camel running swiftly as if into the air of a well, which explains the wording here.
rows.anchor: يقال: هوي نحوه إذا مال، وهوت الناقة تهوي هويا فهي هاوية إذا عدت عدوا شديدا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid say the phrase “hearts of the people” without min would draw Persians, Romans, Turks, Indians, Jews, Christians, and Magians; min restricts the yearning to Muslims, who long to visit the House.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس ومجاهد: لو قال أفئدة الناس لازدحمت عليه فارس والروم والترك والهند واليهود والنصارى والمجوس

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid reads tahwā ilayhim, taking it to mean that people love and revere them.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد «تهوى إليهم» أي تهواهم وتجلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God answered the prayer by growing the trees of al-Taif and bringing fruits to Mecca from other lands.
rows.anchor: فاستجاب الله دعاءه، وأنبت لهم بالطائف سائر الأشجار، وبما يجلب إليهم من الأمصار

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: A report via Yusuf ibn Adi from Ibn Umar says prayer in the Prophet’s Mosque is better than a thousand elsewhere except the Sacred Mosque, where prayer is better than elsewhere.
rows.anchor: حدثنا يوسف بن عدي عن عمر بن عبيد عن عبد الملك عن عطاء عن ابن عمر قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: ابن حبيب
rows.claim: Ibn Habib says Mutarrif and Asbagh, reporting from Ibn Wahb, preferred the Sacred Mosque over the Prophet’s Mosque based on reports in this chapter.
rows.anchor: وذكر ابن حبيب عن مطرف وعن أصبغ

rows.speaker: مالك وسائر العلماء
rows.claim: Malik and the other scholars agree that Eid prayers are held in an open area in every town except Mecca, where they are held in the Sacred Mosque.
rows.anchor: وقد اتفق مالك وسائر العلماء على أن صلاة العيدين يبرز لهما في كل بلد إلا مكة فإنها تصلى في المسجد الحرام

rows.speaker: عمر وعلي وابن مسعود وأبو الدرداء وجابر
rows.claim: Umar, Ali, Ibn Masud, Abu al-Darda, and Jabir preferred Mecca and its mosque; the commentator says they are more worthy to follow, and attributes this view to al-Shafiʿi, Ata, Meccans, Kufans, and a report from Malik.
rows.anchor: وكان عمر وعلي وابن مسعود وأبو الدرداء وجابر يفضلون مكة ومسجدها وهم أولى بالتقليد ممن بعدهم

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: A report from Malik in Ibn Wahb’s Jamiʿ says Adam asked which place God most preferred for worship and was told Mecca.
rows.anchor: ذكر ابن وهب في جامعه عن مالك أن آدم عليه السلام لما أهبط إلى الأرض

rows.speaker: مالك وأهل المدينة
rows.claim: The well-known view of Malik and the people of Medina prefers Medina; Basrans and Baghdadis disagreed, with some favoring Mecca and others Medina.
rows.anchor: والمشهور عنه وعن أهل المدينة تفضيل المدينة، واختلف أهل البصرة والبغداديون في ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: At the end of this segment, the commentator introduces a long Bukhari report from Ibn Abbas, continued in the next segment.
rows.anchor: في صحيح البخاري عن ابن عباس الحديث الطويل وقد ذكرنا بعضه

words: فَٱجْعَلْ أَفْـِٔدَةًۭ مِّنَ ٱلنَّاسِ تَهْوِىٓ إِلَيْهِمْ
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The Bukhari report from Ibn Abbas tells how Abraham visited after Ismail’s first marriage: the wife complained of hardship, so Abraham left a message to change the doorstep; Ismail understood and divorced her.
rows.anchor: فجاء إبراهيم بعد ما تزوج إسمعيل يطالع تركته فلم يجد إسمعيل

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In the same report, Abraham’s second daughter-in-law praises their provision of meat and water; he asks God to bless them, and the Prophet says they had no grain, which Abraham would also have blessed.
rows.anchor: ما طعامكم؟ قالت: اللحم. قال فما شرابكم؟ قالت: الماء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Abraham asked that people yearn to settle in Mecca so it would become a sanctuary.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: قول إبراهيم { فاجعل أفئدة من الناس تهوي إليهم } سأل أن يجعل الله الناس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The Bukhari account says Jurhum were the first to settle there: a caravan saw a bird circling, found Zamzam, and asked Hajar permission to camp, agreeing they had no right to the water; she welcomed company.
rows.anchor: وأول من سكنه جرهم. ففي البخاري بعد قوله: وإن الله لا يضيع أهله وكان البيت مرتفعا من الأرض كالرابية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The Bukhari report continues that Hajar welcomed the company because she wanted companionship; Jurhum settled there with their families, Ismail grew up, and Hajar died before Abraham later visited him.
rows.anchor: فألفى ذلك أم إسمعيل وهي تحب الأنس

words: رَبَّنَآ إِنَّكَ تَعْلَمُ مَا نُخْفِى وَمَا نُعْلِنُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nothing about their circumstances is hidden from God.
rows.anchor: أي ليس يخفى عليك شيء من أحوالنا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومقاتل
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Muqatil say Abraham’s concealed and public feeling was his longing for Ismail and Hajar after settling them in a barren valley.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس ومقاتل: تعلم جميع ما أخفيه وما أعلنه من الوجد بإسمعيل وأمه

words: وَمَا يَخْفَىٰ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ مِن شَىْءٍۢ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ
rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view treats the statement that nothing is hidden from God in earth or heaven as Abraham’s speech.
rows.anchor: قيل: هو من قول إبراهيم

words: وَمَا يَخْفَىٰ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ مِن شَىْءٍۢ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ
rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view makes it God’s response after Abraham says that He knows what they conceal and disclose.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو من قول الله تعالى لما قال إبراهيم: { ربنا إنك تعلم ما نخفي وما نعلن }

words: ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ ٱلَّذِى وَهَبَ لِى عَلَى ٱلْكِبَرِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gift in old age refers to both Abraham’s age and his wife’s age.
rows.anchor: أي على كبر سني وسن امرأتي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Ismail was born when Abraham was ninety-nine, and Isaac when Abraham was one hundred and twelve.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس: ولد له إسمعيل وهو ابن تسع وتسعين سنة، وإسحق وهو ابن مائة واثنتي عشرة سنة

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Said ibn Jubayr says Abraham received the glad tidings of Isaac after reaching one hundred and ten.
rows.anchor: سعيد بن جبير: بشر إبراهيم بإسحق بعد عشر ومائة سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham affirms that his Lord hears prayer.
rows.anchor: إن ربي لسميع الدعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham asks to be among those steadfast in Islam and adherence to its rulings.
rows.anchor: أي من الثابتين على الإسلام والتزام أحكامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He asks God to make some of his descendants people who establish prayer.
rows.anchor: أي واجعل من ذريتي من يقيمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Accept my supplication” means accept my worship; the commentator links it to the call to pray in 40:60 and cites the saying that supplication is the marrow of worship.
rows.anchor: وقال ربكم ادعوني أستجب لكم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view says Abraham sought forgiveness for his parents before it was established that they were enemies of God.
rows.anchor: قيل: استغفر إبراهيم لوالديه قبل أن يثبت عنده أنهما عدوان لله

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri says it is possible that Abraham’s mother was Muslim, since God mentions his excuse concerning his father but not his mother.
rows.anchor: القشيري: ولا يبعد أن تكون أمه مسلمة لأن الله ذكر عذره في استغفاره لأبيه دون أمه

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: On that interpretation, Said ibn Jubayr reads the phrase as “my father,” referring to his father alone.
rows.anchor: قراءة سعيد بن جبير، { رب اغفر لي ولوالدي } يعني أباه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other views say Abraham prayed for his parents hoping they would believe, or conditionally upon their becoming Muslim.
rows.anchor: وقيل: استغفر لهما طمعا في إيمانهما. وقيل: استغفر لهما بشرط أن يسلما

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says the parents Abraham meant were Adam and Eve.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أراد آدم وحواء. وقد روي

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A separate view says Abraham meant his sons Ismail and Isaac.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه أراد ولديه إسمعيل وإسحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says that prayer for deceased unbelieving parents is redirected to Adam and Eve, since they are the parents of all humanity.
rows.anchor: وقد روي أن العبد إذا قال: اللهم اغفر لي ولوالدي وكان أبواه قد ماتا كافرين

rows.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي ويحيى بن يعمر
rows.claim: Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi and Yahya ibn Yaʿmar read “my two sons,” meaning Ismail and Isaac; al-Mawardi and al-Nahhas mention the reading.
rows.anchor: وكان إبراهيم النخعي يقرأ: «ولولدي» يعني ابنيه، وكذلك قرأ يحيى بن يعمر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas takes “the believers” to mean the community of Muhammad.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس: من أمة محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view includes all believers, which the commentator considers the more evident meaning.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «للمؤمنين» كلهم وهو أظهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The day the reckoning stands is the day people rise for the account.
rows.anchor: أي يوم يقوم الناس للحساب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the people to be warned are the inhabitants of Mecca.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس: أراد أهل مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The day the punishment comes is the Day of Resurrection; punishment is emphasized because the passage threatens sinners, although the day also brings reward.
rows.anchor: وهو يوم القيامة أي خوفهم ذلك اليوم. وإنما خصهم بيوم العذاب وإن كان يوم الثواب، لأن الكلام خرج مخرج التهديد للعاصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who wronged are the people speaking on that day.
rows.anchor: أي في ذلك اليوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Akhkhirna means give us respite.
rows.anchor: أي أمهلنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once the truth appears in the afterlife, they ask to be returned to worldly life for a short time.
rows.anchor: سألوه الرجوع إلى الدنيا حين ظهر الحق في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They promise to answer God’s call to Islam.
rows.anchor: أي إلى الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They promise to follow the messengers.
rows.anchor: ونتبع الرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s reply recalls their oaths made in worldly life.
rows.anchor: يعني في دار الدنيا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says Quraysh swore that they would not be resurrected.
rows.anchor: مجاهد: هو قسم قريش أنهم لا يبعثون

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj connects the oath to the statement in 16:38 that they swore forcefully that God would not resurrect the dead.
rows.anchor: ابن جريج: هو ما حكاه عنهم في قوله

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: One interpretation of “no departure” is that there is no transition from worldly life to the afterlife, meaning no resurrection or gathering.
rows.anchor: أحدهما ما لكم من انتقال عن الدنيا إلى الآخرة أي لا تبعثون ولا تحشرون وهذا قول مجاهد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A second interpretation says “no departure” means no escape from the punishment.
rows.anchor: الثاني { ما لكم من زوال } أي من العذاب

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Al-Bayhaqi reports Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi’s account that Hell’s people make five requests, receiving answers to four before never speaking again: 40:11–12, 32:12–14, this plea, and 35:37 with God’s reply.
rows.anchor: وذكر البيهقي عن محمد بن كعب القرظي قال: لأهل النار خمس دعوات يجيبهم الله في أربعة
